title: Eighteen schools
hook: the early schools multiplied, each with its own reading of the texts

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sthaviras and the great community, and three stories of why they parted. Your line: accounts differ. Today, the branches keep branching.

Eighteen. That's the number the old chronicles give for the schools that grew up after the first split. The trouble is, when you put the lists side by side, they don't name the same eighteen. Some lists have more names than that. Some schools appear under two names. The number stays the same while the names shift around it, as if eighteen were less a count than a way of saying: a whole family of schools.
screen: `EIGHTEEN, SAY THE CHRONICLES.` → `THE LISTS DON'T MATCH.` → `A WHOLE FAMILY OF SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: These weren't separate religions. A school, a nikaya, was a community of monks with its own lineage, its own copy of the discipline, and often its own way of reading the teaching. A few of the readings: the Sarvastivada taught that all things exist in the past, present and future, and their name is read as those who say all exists. Another family of schools, the Pudgalavadins, held that there is a person, a pudgala, which is neither the same as the parts of body and mind nor separate from them. The Lokottaravada, a branch of the great community, taught that the Buddha's life in the world was in a deep sense beyond the world. The Theravada called itself the teaching of the elders. How did they argue? The Theravada canon even contains a book, the Kathavatthu, that sets out points of controversy as question and answer: a position is stated, questioned, and answered. It is written from the Theravada side, but it preserves the questions other schools were asking. Today the Theravada continues as a living school with its canon in Pali, and the discipline codes of other early schools still guide monks and nuns in East Asia and Tibet. Each of these schools kept faith with the texts the way its teachers had, and each, the Theravada included, understood itself as keeping the Buddha's teaching whole.
screen: `A SCHOOL WAS A LINEAGE.` · `ALL EXISTS, A PERSON, BEYOND THE WORLD.` · `POINTS OF CONTROVERSY.` · `STILL CARRIED TODAY.` · then, large: `MANY READINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of a text, a family saying or even a recipe that you and someone else read differently, and say their reading to yourself as fairly as you can. Then find one thing in it you can respect, what it protects or what it notices that yours might miss.
Eighteen schools. The chronicles' name for the early schools that grew from the first split, each with its own reading of the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: many readings. Eighteen was less a count than a family. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics today are ordained in lineages whose discipline codes trace back to particular early schools, and students of Buddhism read the early schools' debates in texts like the Kathavatthu.

chat.says: Were the eighteen schools like separate religions?
options: No: each was a monks' lineage with its own discipline and reading.
Yes: each one followed a different founder instead of the Buddha.
No: they were eighteen buildings of one big monastery.
chat.meaning: A school, a nikaya, was a community of monks with its own lineage, discipline code and often its own reading of the teaching.

sources.ref: Vasumitra, treatise on the doctrines of the schools

notes: 'Eighteen' is attributed to the chronicles (Dipavamsa 5 counts the Theravada plus seventeen others). 'Some lists have more names than that' and 'some schools appear under two names' compare Dipavamsa and Vasumitra; confirm.

School summaries are one line each and deliberately simple: Sarvastivada (dharmas exist in the three times); Pudgalavada (pudgala neither identical with nor different from the aggregates); Lokottaravada (the Buddha's worldly life as supramundane); Theravada as Vibhajjavada. Confirm fairness.

'Monks of different schools could live in the same region, sometimes in the same monastery': supported by later pilgrim reports (e.g. Xuanzang, Yijing), not by the cited texts; Keeper may want it softened or cut.

'The Theravada continues today as a living school with its canon in Pali' (no 'only' claim): a description of the present, not a ranking; confirm wording does not read as a ranking. East Asian (Dharmaguptaka) and Tibetan (Mulasarvastivada) Vinayas named only generally.

Editor pass: cut 'rival churches' (borrowed Christian framing), the shared-monastery claim (not in the cited texts), and 'school of analysis' (from the commentaries, not the cited texts); Sarvastivada name given as a reading rather than an etymology.

Audit (serious): the closing claim that the early teaching 'wasn't one voice that later fell apart' had the narrator take a side on a contested historical question, against the Theravada self-understanding; replaced with a description of how each school saw itself. Keeper to confirm wording.
